paras: The lynching of Ed Sayles was the hanging of a Black youth by a masked band at Iredell, Texas, on the night of July 6, 1882. Sayles, accused that morning of raping a farmer's wife, was taken from his guards and hanged from a pecan tree near the depot. The wire carried the story across the country, often under headlines that approved the killing.

Sayles, described as about 18 years old and "a small, black negro," had lived for several months with W. J. Pugh, a farmer about four miles northwest of Iredell. According to the Iredell correspondent of the Waco Examiner and the Dallas Herald, Pugh went hunting after breakfast on July 6, and Sayles was accused of raping Mrs. Pugh at about 7 a.m., using a knife to intimidate her. The same report added that Mrs. Pugh was "not seriously injured."

A neighbor woman saw Sayles "skulking through the brush" and raised an alarm, and neighbors caught him in Iredell. He was taken to the Pugh house to be identified, but because Mrs. Pugh was "much indisposed" the examination was put off until evening, when he was to be taken to the jail at Meridian. Meanwhile a crowd gathered in town, "some talk of lynching was heard," and Constable Tidwell kept Sayles under guard.

At 11 o'clock that night a "masked band of a dozen men" broke in the doors of the building where Sayles was confined and, after a short scuffle with the guards, took him to a pecan tree near the depot and hanged him. The Waco Examiner's correspondent wrote that "no fuss was made, but the avengers seemed to do the work thoroughly," and that the town was quiet.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official inquiry into the hanging appears in the coverage.

The first accounts were same-day specials from Iredell printed on July 7 by the Waco Daily Examiner and the Dallas Daily Herald, which the Dallas Weekly Herald repeated on July 13. These local reports gave the most detail, naming Sayles, Mrs. Pugh and the constable, and calling the lynchers "the avengers."

Two wire versions dated July 7 spread the story outside Texas, one a three-sentence item and the other a fuller account credited by the Bismarck Tribune to the St. Louis Republican. Papers in Sacramento, St. Paul, Salt Lake City, Eureka, Sedalia, Canton and Bismarck printed them between July 8 and 14, under headlines such as "Killed for Cause," "Got His Just Deserts," "A Negro's Just Fate" and "Deservedly Lynched." Transmission garbled names and places: Iredell became "Inedell," "Tredell," "Ivadell" and "Indell," and the Salt Lake Herald called the victim "Taylor."

By mid-July the case had shrunk to one-line items in news-summary columns, some dated July 7 and some joking about the hanging. The Elko Independent wrote that "the brute" had "stood upon nothing and pointed at the milky-way with his nose," and a syndicated column printed in Minnesota said he "went over the range at the hands of Judge Lynch."

The local Iredell specials say Sayles was still held in Iredell awaiting transfer when the band came, while the wire versions say he had been taken to the jail at Meridian and was taken from there. The wires also put the tree 300 yards from the depot rather than 100 and printed the accuser's initials variously as W. P., S. W. and W. A.; the same-day local reports are the closer source.

bases: A masked band of about a dozen men broke into the building where the accused Sayles was held under guard and hanged him from a pecan tree (A1, A2, A4).
Sayles, accused of rape, was taken from guards by a masked band of a dozen men and hanged without trial (A1, A2); the papers called it a lynching and the men 'avengers' (A1, A3, A15).

The Iredell specials to the Waco Examiner and Dallas Herald (A1, A2) and two differently worded wire versions (A3, A4/A12) agree that Sayles was taken from custody by masked men and hanged, though all may trace to one Iredell correspondent.

accounts.label: Iredell correspondent (Texas specials)
accounts.gist: Neighbors caught Sayles in Iredell; identification was postponed; he was guarded by Constable Tidwell pending removal to the Meridian jail that evening, and at 11 o'clock a masked band of a dozen broke into the building where he was confined and hanged him near the depot.

framing.detail: The Texas specials called the lynchers 'the avengers' who 'seemed to do the work thoroughly' and reported 'The town is quiet'.
Out-of-state headlines read 'Killed for Cause', 'Got His Just Deserts', 'A Negro's Just Fate' and 'Deservedly Lynched'.
Brief items joked that Sayles 'stood upon nothing and pointed at the milky-way with his nose' or 'went over the range at the hands of Judge Lynch'.
Short wire items under 'Negro Lynched' and 'A Ravisher Lynched' gave the facts in three sentences.
